ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Cognitive Neurology Consultation — Emile Griffith

code.originalText: Two-week review, seen the same day by cognitive neurology: brain MRI, staging, traumatic encephalopathy syndrome and other causes, sertraline and sodium

text.paragraph: About a year of memory loss and confusion in a retired professional boxer of 67 with a long career, a severe assault with a head injury thirteen years ago, and chronic PTSD; MoCA 22. Please stage the impairment, weigh traumatic brain injury and traumatic encephalopathy syndrome against Alzheimer's disease, vascular disease and the effects of PTSD and depression, and advise on further testing, treatment and safety. [S]
Urgency: Routine; at the memory clinic two weeks from now, on the same day as his two-week primary care visit, with brain MRI that morning. [S]

list.item: What is the stage of his impairment, and what pattern does it show?

How likely are traumatic brain injury and traumatic encephalopathy syndrome as the cause, compared with Alzheimer's disease or vascular disease, and how much might PTSD, depression and sleep be adding?
Which further tests do you advise: neuropsychological testing, Alzheimer's disease biomarkers, or others?
Is any medicine for cognition indicated, and is sertraline a reasonable choice for his PTSD from a cognitive point of view?
What do you advise for safety when he travels, for falls, and for support for his care partner?

text.paragraph: Mr. Griffith, 67, was seen with his care partner, who gave a consistent account with his permission. He boxed professionally for nineteen years, in 112 bouts, and cannot count the knockdowns or the times he was dazed. Thirteen years ago he was badly beaten and spent months in hospital; he and his care partner date the first memory lapses to that time, with a slow worsening over the past year rather than a sudden change. He now loses the thread of conversations, needs reminders, and finds names slow to come, though the names come with a hint. He has no headaches, seizures, tremor, change in walking beyond some unsteadiness, change in smell, dream enactment, hallucinations, impulsive behavior, rages or paranoia. He has nightmares about the title fight most nights and guilt about it, and sleeps about five hours. He started sertraline 25 mg two weeks ago, with nausea for three days that has passed. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Emile Alphonse Griffith was born on February 3, 1938, in St. Thomas, U.S. Virgin Islands, one of eight children. [D]
He moved to New York City as a young man and turned professional in 1958. [D]

He boxed professionally for nineteen years, from 1958 to 1977, in 112 bouts (a record of 85 wins, 24 losses and 2 draws), won five world titles at welterweight and middleweight, was the first boxer from the U.S. Virgin Islands to become a world champion, and retired at 39, after losing his last three fights; he entered the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 1990. [D]

On March 24, 1962, at Madison Square Garden, he regained the welterweight title by stopping Benny Paret in the twelfth round; Paret never regained consciousness, had emergency brain surgery, and died ten days later. Sports Illustrated reported in 2005 that an anti-gay slur Paret directed at him at the weigh-in may have fueled him. [D]

The fight's outcome stayed with him for decades. His biographer said he saw visions of Paret at night and in a mirror and refused to box again for months; Griffith said he was "never the same fighter after that"; and in a documentary released in 2005 he told Paret's son, "Sometimes I still have nightmares." [D]

The project roster describes post-traumatic stress disorder from the ring death. No source read records that diagnosis; the documented nightmares, visions and lasting distress are consistent with it only as a retrospective interpretation. [R]

Over the years he described himself at various times as straight, gay and bisexual; in a 2005 interview with Sports Illustrated he said, "I don't know what I am." His biographer said he lived openly, going to gay bars, but did not say so publicly until after the 2005 documentary about him. [D]

In 1992 he was attacked and badly beaten by a group of men, one with a baseball bat, after leaving a gay bar in midtown Manhattan near Times Square; he spent several months in hospital, much of it in intensive care. The motive was never established. [D]
A 2005 review of the documentary reported that he had had short-term memory problems since the 1992 attack. [D]
After boxing he trained other boxers, including world champions, and worked as a corrections officer and a bartender. [D]

text.paragraph: 2 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.

tr.td: Sertraline 25 mg oral tablet, one tablet each morning

Memory loss and confusion over about a year, worse in recent months, reported by him and his care partner: repeating stories and questions, losing the thread of conversations, mixing up days, two missed appointments, and once getting lost changing trains on a familiar route; cause to be found
S — Synthetic presenting problem anchored to the documented short-term memory problems; resolved into the diagnosis at the third visit. Not a claim about his real symptoms at that age.

Post-traumatic stress disorder, chronic, after two index events (a title fight decades ago after which his opponent died, and a severe assault thirteen years ago): nightmares, unwanted images, avoidance of fight footage, guilt and self-blame, being on guard in crowds, poor sleep; PCL-5 41
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis at intake by clinical interview against DSM-5-TR criteria, anchored to his public words about lifelong nightmares; not a historical diagnosis.
Personal history of traumatic brain injury: repetitive head impacts over 112 professional bouts, and a severe head injury in an assault thirteen years ago with months in hospital
S — Synthetic coding of the documented career and assault.

text.paragraph: Vital signs recorded on 2026-05-19; see the referring visit's Vital Signs section. [S]

tr.td: Well and warm; blood pressure 130/78 mmHg; pulse 68
Oriented except for the date; slow to retrieve the plan from intake but recalls it with cues; Clinical Dementia Rating global 0.5 (sum of boxes 2.0) from interviews with him and his care partner
Normal, including smell, eye movements and facial strength
Normal tone and strength; no tremor, rigidity or slowness of movement

code.displayName: Relevant Diagnostic Tests and/or Laboratory Data

list.item: Mild cognitive impairment (CDR 0.5) of frontal-subcortical pattern (R41.3). Slowed processing, poor set-shifting and retrieval that improves with cues, with preserved independence in daily life, fit mild cognitive impairment (mild neurocognitive disorder), not dementia. [S]

Traumatic brain injury and traumatic encephalopathy syndrome (Z87.820). Repetitive head impacts over a long career and the severe assault are the most likely causes; the MRI shows an old right frontal injury, frontal microbleeds and a cavum septi pellucidi, and spares the hippocampi. He probably meets the NINDS 2021 criteria for traumatic encephalopathy syndrome (substantial exposure, a core cognitive impairment, a progressive course, not fully accounted for by another condition). These are research criteria: they cannot confirm chronic traumatic encephalopathy in life, they are not a clinical diagnosis, and they do not change treatment. The single severe injury makes it impossible to separate the two exposures. [S]

Alzheimer's disease and vascular disease. Alzheimer's disease is less likely given the retrieval pattern and normal hippocampi, but co-pathology at 67 cannot be excluded. Vascular change is slight (Fazekas 1, no infarct). [S]

Chronic PTSD, depressive symptoms and short sleep (F43.12). These can impair attention and retrieval and are treatable; treating them is the best chance of improving his day-to-day thinking. Sertraline is a reasonable choice: it has no anticholinergic burden; sodium and falls need watching. Benzodiazepines, sedating sleep aids and anticholinergic drugs should be avoided. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Fairbanks-Ochieng's intake note: MoCA 22, PHQ-9 9, PC-PTSD-5 4, PCL-5 41, Functional Activities Questionnaire 6, Timed Up and Go 13 seconds, normal blood count, metabolic panel, B12 and TSH; sodium 138 mmol/L today, two weeks into sertraline. Brain MRI this morning, reviewed with the images: mild generalized atrophy, more in the frontal lobes; hippocampi in the normal range for age (medial temporal atrophy score 1 on each side); a small old injury (encephalomalacia with hemosiderin) at the tip of the right frontal lobe; seven microbleeds at the gray-white junction of both frontal lobes; Fazekas 1 white matter change; a cavum septi pellucidi; no infarct, mass, subdural collection or hydrocephalus. [S]

list.item: Neuropsychological testing in about three weeks to define the pattern, confirm the stage and give a baseline for follow-up. [S]

Alzheimer's disease biomarker testing (blood, CSF or amyloid PET) can be offered after the testing; it is optional if the result would not change his care, and with seven microbleeds he would not be a candidate for anti-amyloid antibodies whatever the result. [S]
No cholinesterase inhibitor or memantine: neither is shown to help mild cognitive impairment or traumatic brain injury. [S]

Continue sertraline and raise to 50 mg at six weeks if tolerated, with a sodium check two to four weeks after the change; continue cognitive processing therapy, adapted with written summaries, reminders and his care partner's help between sessions. [S]
Memory strategies: one calendar, phone reminders and a fixed routine; daily exercise, social activity and regular sleep. [S]
Safety: an address card, shared phone location and company on unfamiliar routes; shared oversight of bills; physical therapy for balance as already ordered. [S]
Support for his care partner: education, the Alzheimer's Association helpline and a caregiver class; the GUIDE model applies only if dementia develops. [S]
Advance care planning soon, while he can take part fully. [S]

Repeat cognitive testing yearly and neuropsychological testing in twelve to eighteen months, or sooner with change; return to the memory clinic for faster decline, parkinsonism, behavioral change or a fall with head injury. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Fairbanks-Ochieng, who saw him the same day. The findings were explained to him and his care partner in plain words; he agreed to neuropsychological testing and wants to hear the results with his care partner present. [S]

Follow-up: Dr. Fairbanks-Ochieng will review the testing with him at the six-week visit and continue his care; the memory clinic will see him again in about a year with repeat testing, or sooner with any of the changes above. [S]
